uses: Thyme is best known in tradition as a chest herb. A warm infusion sweetened with honey was the old household standby for coughs with phlegm, colds and a sore throat, and Culpeper ranked it among the best herbs for the lungs and for whooping cough. It was also taken after meals for wind and colic. The Greeks burned it as incense, and in the age of chivalry it stood for courage. In the kitchen it flavors stuffings, stews, soups and sauces.
energetics: Culpeper called thyme hot and dry in the third degree
caution_pregnancy: Safety during pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the EMA does not recommend medicinal thyme or thyme oil then. Not enough is known; avoid medicinal amounts. Culpeper's old claims that thyme brings on periods and labor are a further reason for care.
caution_medications: The EMA reports no known interactions for thyme or thyme oil. Few studies have looked, so check with a pharmacist if you take regular medicines.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to thyme or to other mint-family (Lamiaceae) plants, such as sage, rosemary or basil. See a doctor if a cough brings shortness of breath, fever or pus-colored phlegm. Thyme medicines are not established for young children; most aren't recommended under 12, and most thyme oil products aren't recommended under 18. Take care with full hot baths if you have high blood pressure, and skip them with a high fever, open wounds or large skin injuries, an acute skin disease, severe infection, serious circulation problems or heart failure. Taken by mouth, thyme can upset the stomach.
caution_duration: If a cough lasts longer than a week, or gets worse, see a doctor or qualified practitioner.
caution_topical: Thyme oil can irritate the skin and cause allergic reactions; Grieve notes thymol stings skin and mucous membranes. Never put thyme oil on the face, especially near the nose, of babies and children under 2, because it can trigger a dangerous spasm of the voice box (laryngospasm).
garden_harvest_timing: Cut the leafy tops just before the plant flowers, when the oil is strongest, and leave the woody base with a few inches of green so it regrows.
garden_water: Dry; needs sharp drainage and dislikes wet soil
notes: A low, woody evergreen that likes dry, stony, neutral to alkaline soil. Seed germinates unevenly, so cuttings, layering or division are easier. Trim it when it gets leggy. Bees love the flowers; Grieve suggests planting thyme near hives. Culpeper calls thyme a notable herb of Venus; he places wild thyme (Thymus serpyllum) under Venus and Aries.
